breakfast.name: Caldo de Mancarra (Peanut Porridge)
instructions: Cook rice until very soft
Add ground peanuts
Simmer until thick porridge
Sweeten with sugar

breakfast.name: Fried Plantains with Bread
instructions: Slice and fry plantains
Toast bread with butter
Serve together
breakfast.description: Simple breakfast of fried plantains and bread.

breakfast.name: Mingau de Arroz (Rice Porridge)
instructions: Cook rice in coconut milk on low heat, stirring often
Cook until very soft and porridge-like — 15-20 min
Add sugar, cinnamon, lime zest
The coconut milk makes it rich and creamy
Serve warm — this is comfort breakfast in Guinea-Bissau
The Portuguese 'mingau' tradition adapted with West African coconut
Simple, cheap, nourishing — the national morning bowl
breakfast.description: Guinea-Bissau's morning rice porridge — rice cooked in coconut milk until creamy, spiced with cinnamon and lime. The Portuguese colonial porridge tradition adapted with West African coconut and tropical flavors.

breakfast.name: Pão com Manteiga e Café (Bread with Butter and Coffee)
ingredients: Strong coffee (Guinea-Bissau grows cashew, not coffee, but the café culture is Portuguese-inherited)
instructions: Slice bread, spread with butter
Make strong coffee — add sugar liberally
Add condensed milk to coffee for the Lusophone African style
Dip bread in coffee — a Portuguese-African morning ritual
The simplicity is the point — fresh bread, good butter, strong sweet coffee
This Portuguese breakfast survived colonialism and became Bissau-Guinean
Every morning in Bissau starts with pão and café
breakfast.description: The simplest and most daily breakfast in Guinea-Bissau — crusty Portuguese bread with butter, dipped in strong sweet coffee. A Portuguese colonial inheritance that became deeply Bissau-Guinean. Every morning in Bissau starts here.

lunch.name: Caldo de Chabéu (Palm Oil Rice)
instructions: Sauté onion and tomato in palm oil
Add rice and water
Cook until rice is done
Serve with fried fish

lunch.name: Jollof Rice
instructions: Brown chicken
Sauté onion, tomatoes, paste
Add rice and water
Cook covered until done
lunch.description: Tomato-stewed rice with chicken — West African classic.

lunch.name: Caldo de Mancarra (Peanut Soup)
ingredients: Peanuts (roasted, ground into a paste) or natural peanut butter
instructions: Brown meat in palm oil
Sauté onion, garlic, tomato until soft
Add peanut paste — stir until dissolved into the broth
Add water, sweet potato, Scotch bonnet
Simmer 35-40 min until meat is tender and soup is thick
The peanut makes the soup creamy, rich, and slightly sweet
The palm oil adds depth and that characteristic red-orange color
Serve over or alongside rice
This is Guinea-Bissau's version of the West African groundnut soup — heartier, soupier
lunch.description: Guinea-Bissau's peanut soup — roasted ground peanuts dissolved into a rich, thick broth with meat and sweet potato. The Lusophone West African version of groundnut soup, made heartier and soupier than its neighbors' stews. The peanut-palm oil combination is liquid comfort.

lunch.name: Arroz de Chabéu (Monkey Bread Rice)
ingredients: Chabéu fruit (baobab fruit — the monkey bread tree)
instructions: Process chabéu (baobab fruit): break open the hard shell, soak the chalky pulp in water
Strain the baobab water — it's tangy, slightly sour, rich in vitamin C
Cook rice in the baobab water — it gives the rice a unique tangy flavor
In separate pot, make a sauce with palm oil, onion, tomato paste, fish/meat
Combine or serve the baobab rice with the sauce
The tanginess of the baobab transforms ordinary rice
Baobab is iconic to the African landscape — the 'upside down tree'
This is one of Guinea-Bissau's most distinctive dishes — not found outside the region
lunch.description: Rice cooked in baobab fruit water — one of Guinea-Bissau's most unique dishes. The tangy, vitamin-C-rich baobab gives the rice a flavor found nowhere else. The baobab tree (Africa's 'tree of life') and this rice preparation are viral food anthropology.

lunch.name: Caldeirada de Peixe (Fish Stew)
ingredients: Fresh fish (whole or fillets — whatever's freshest from the Bissau coast)
instructions: Layer fish with sliced tomato, onion, green pepper in a pot
Add olive oil, lime juice, parsley
Add wine if using, or water
Simmer gently 25-30 min — don't stir aggressively, the fish should hold its shape
The stew should be brothy but rich with fish flavor
Add potatoes if desired — they cook in the broth
The Portuguese caldeirada technique adapted with West African fish and flavors
Serve in deep bowls with bread for soaking up the broth
Guinea-Bissau's coast provides incredible fish — this stew lets the fish speak
lunch.description: Guinea-Bissau's fish stew — fresh coastal fish layered with tomatoes, onions, and olive oil in a Portuguese caldeirada adapted for West Africa. Where Portuguese fishing tradition meets one of West Africa's richest coastlines.

dinner.name: Caldo de Peixe (Fish Stew)
instructions: Marinate fish in lime
Sauté onion, tomatoes in palm oil
Add fish and water
Simmer 20 min
Garnish with cilantro

dinner.name: Chicken Yassa
instructions: Marinate chicken in lemon, onion, garlic
Brown chicken
Cook onions until soft
Add mustard, return chicken
Simmer 20 min

dinner.name: Galinha Grelhada com Piripiri (Grilled Chicken with Piri Piri)
ingredients: Piri piri sauce: bird's eye chilies, garlic, lemon juice, oil, paprika, oregano
instructions: Make piri piri: blend chilies, garlic, lemon, oil, paprika, oregano — it should be fiery and bright
Marinate butterflied chicken in piri piri — minimum 2 hours, overnight is better
Grill over charcoal — low and slow, skin side up first
Turn frequently, basting with more piri piri
The skin should be charred and crispy, the meat juicy and spice-stained red
The charcoal and the piri piri are both non-negotiable — this is not an oven dish
Serve with lime wedges and rice or fries
Guinea-Bissau's piri piri is Portuguese-origin but West African in heat level
This is the dish that put Lusophone Africa on the global food map
dinner.description: Piri piri chicken — the dish that connects Portugal, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, and Angola in one fiery package. Butterflied chicken marinated in chili-garlic-lemon paste and charcoal-grilled until charred and juicy. The Lusophone African food chain's most globally viral dish.

dinner.name: Cozido de Cabrito (Goat Stew)
instructions: Season goat with garlic, pepper, bay leaf — marinate 1 hour
Brown goat in palm oil until deeply colored
Add onion, tomato, cook until soft
Add water, bring to simmer
Cook low and slow 45-60 min — goat needs time
Add sweet potato and cassava in the last 20 min
The root vegetables absorb the goat-palm oil broth
The stew should be thick, rich, and deeply flavored
Goat is Guinea-Bissau's most important meat — this stew is daily home cooking
dinner.description: Guinea-Bissau's everyday goat stew — bone-in goat slow-cooked in palm oil with sweet potato and cassava. Goat is the country's most important meat, and this stew is what home cooking smells like in Bissau.

dinner.name: Arroz de Tomate (Tomato Rice)
instructions: Fry onion, garlic in oil until golden
Add tomato paste, fry until dark and oil separates
Add fresh chopped tomatoes, cook until broken down
Add fish or chicken, cook briefly
Add water, bring to boil, add rice
Cover and cook on low 20-25 min until rice absorbs all liquid
The rice should be tomato-red and each grain separate
Bay leaf adds a subtle background note
This is Guinea-Bissau's Portuguese-influenced one-pot rice — simpler than jollof, equally satisfying
dinner.description: Guinea-Bissau's tomato rice — rice cooked in a rich tomato base with fish or chicken. The Portuguese arroz de tomate tradition adapted with palm oil and West African technique. Simpler than jollof, deeply satisfying, and everyday Bissau-Guinean food.

snacks.name: Pastéis de Peixe (Fish Pastries)
instructions: Make pastry, roll circles
Fill with cooked fish mixture
Fold and seal
Fry until golden

snacks.name: Cajú Assado (Roasted Cashews)
ingredients: Raw cashews (Guinea-Bissau is one of the world's largest cashew producers)
instructions: Guinea-Bissau is Africa's top cashew exporter — the nuts grow everywhere
Roast raw cashews in a dry pan or oven — 10-15 min at 175°C
Toss with salt — and chili if desired
The roasting brings out the buttery sweetness
Most of Guinea-Bissau's cashews are exported raw — roasting locally is a growing movement
The cashew nut grows hanging below the cashew apple — each fruit produces just one nut
Every September-November is cashew season — the country runs on it
These are fresher and sweeter than any store-bought cashew
snacks.description: Guinea-Bissau's cashew nuts — freshly roasted from one of the world's largest cashew-producing countries. The country's economy runs on cashew exports. The 'one fruit, one nut' harvest and the farm-to-mouth freshness make Bissau-Guinean cashews a viral food-origin story.

snacks.name: Pastéis de Bacalhau (Salt Cod Fritters)
instructions: Soak salt cod overnight, boil, flake — remove all bones
Boil potatoes, mash
Mix flaked cod, mashed potato, egg, minced onion, parsley
Shape into oval croquettes
Deep fry until golden — 3-4 min
Drain briefly — serve hot
These are a direct import from Portugal — bacalhau is sacred in Lusophone cooking
Guinea-Bissau's version is exactly the Portuguese recipe — proof of cultural persistence
The crispy shell and the salty-potato interior are addictive
snacks.description: Pastéis de bacalhau — Portugal's iconic salt cod fritters, transplanted intact to Guinea-Bissau. Flaked salt cod and mashed potato fried into golden croquettes. One of the clearest examples of Portuguese culinary colonialism surviving in West Africa.

snacks.name: Sumo de Cajú (Cashew Apple Juice)
ingredients: Cashew apples (the fruit — most people only know the nut)
instructions: The cashew apple is the fruit that the cashew nut hangs from — juicy, tangy, slightly astringent
Wash and squeeze cashew apples — they're very juicy
Blend with water, strain
Add sugar and lime juice
Chill — serve ice cold
The flavor is unique — tangy, slightly astringent, tropical
Most of the world throws away the cashew apple and keeps only the nut
In Guinea-Bissau, the fruit is valued as much as the nut — juice, wine, jam
This is cashew-season refreshment — September to November
snacks.description: Cashew apple juice — the juice from the fruit most of the world throws away to get the nut. In Guinea-Bissau, the tangy, tropical cashew apple is prized for juice, wine, and jam. The 'the fruit of the cashew' surprise and the zero-waste angle are viral.

desserts.name: Dodol (Coconut Fudge)
instructions: Mix rice flour with coconut milk
Cook with sugar, stirring constantly
When very thick and pulling from pan, pour into mold
Cool and slice

desserts.name: Pudim de Leite (Milk Pudding/Flan)
instructions: Make caramel: melt sugar until amber, pour into mold — coat bottom and sides
Mix eggs, condensed milk, milk, vanilla — whisk until smooth
Pour custard over caramel in the mold
Bake in a water bath (bain-marie) at 160°C for 35-40 min
The custard should be just set — jiggly but not liquid
Chill completely — overnight is best
Unmold: the caramel creates a glossy sauce over the smooth custard
The wobble of a perfect flan is mesmerizing — and a test of skill
This is the Portuguese dessert that Guinea-Bissau made its own
desserts.description: Guinea-Bissau's pudim de leite — the Portuguese crème caramel that became West Africa's most elegant dessert. Silky egg custard inverted over a pool of amber caramel. The wobble, the caramel pour, and the Lusophone-African dessert tradition are viral.

desserts.name: Doce de Papaia (Papaya Jam/Sweet)
instructions: Peel and grate green papaya
Cook with sugar, water, cinnamon, cloves — stir frequently
Add lime juice
Cook until thick, translucent, and jammy — 25-30 min
The papaya becomes almost crystallized in the sugar
Serve as a dessert on its own or with bread or cheese
This is the Portuguese doce tradition — preserving tropical fruit in sugar
The green papaya transforms completely — from firm white to translucent amber
desserts.description: Guinea-Bissau's green papaya sweet — unripe papaya cooked in sugar syrup with cinnamon until translucent and jammy. The Portuguese preserve tradition applied to tropical West African fruit. The transformation from plain white papaya to amber jewel is beautiful.

drinks.name: Caju Juice (Cashew Apple Juice)
instructions: Press juice from cashew apples
Strain
Sweeten, add lemon
Serve cold
drinks.description: Tangy juice from the cashew fruit.

drinks.name: Cana (Sugarcane Spirit)
instructions: Press sugarcane
Ferment juice
Distill

drinks.name: Vinho de Cajú (Cashew Wine)
instructions: Squeeze ripe cashew apples — extract all the juice
Add sugar — the amount determines the sweetness and eventual alcohol level
Let ferment naturally for 3-7 days — wild yeasts do the work
Guinea-Bissau's cashew wine is a living fermentation tradition
The fermentation produces a mildly alcoholic, slightly fizzy, tangy wine
Strain before serving
Drink young — this is not meant to age
Cashew wine is ceremonial and social — drunk at gatherings and celebrations
The spontaneous fermentation (no added yeast) is ancient food technology
drinks.description: Guinea-Bissau's cashew wine — cashew apple juice naturally fermented into a mildly alcoholic, tangy wine. The country's most traditional alcoholic drink, made during cashew season with no added yeast. The wild-fermentation technique and the cashew-country origin make this viral fermentation content.

drinks.name: Chá de Cidreira (Lemongrass Tea)
instructions: Bruise lemongrass stalks — crush with the back of a knife
Boil water, add lemongrass
Steep 10 min — the tea turns pale yellow-green
Strain, add sugar or honey
Add lime if desired
Serve hot or cold — both are common
Lemongrass grows wild in Guinea-Bissau — it's free and everywhere
The citrusy, calming flavor is the after-dinner standard
Also considered medicinal — good for digestion and calm
drinks.description: Lemongrass tea — Guinea-Bissau's after-dinner staple, made from lemongrass that grows wild everywhere. Pale, citrusy, calming. A simple pleasure that represents the quiet side of West African food culture.
